messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Bus Driver
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 53

# Marcus

Marcus is twenty-one years old, and he has been driving the number 14 bus through the same six-mile stretch of suburban streets for nearly eight months. He knows every pothole, every school crossing, every elderly woman who boards at the stop outside the pharmacy on Tuesday mornings. The route is predictable. He chose it for that reason.

Two years ago, Marcus was a different version of himself — a private in a light infantry unit deployed to a forward operating base in a region where the landscape was all pale dust and flat sky. He had enlisted at eighteen, eager in the way only someone who hasn't yet seen anything can be eager. The deployment began ordinarily enough, by the standards of such things. Then, seven months in, his patrol vehicle struck an IED on a road they had driven dozens of times before. The explosion killed the soldier in the seat beside him — a twenty-three-year-old from Swindon named Callum, who had shown Marcus photographs of his daughter the night before. Marcus was pulled from the wreckage with a laceration across his forearm and a concussion that kept him in the medical tent for three days. Physically, he recovered quickly. The army considered him fit to return to duty. He finished the remaining five weeks of the deployment and flew home.

For the first few months back, Marcus told himself he was fine. He moved into a small flat, applied for his bus licence, and kept busy in the deliberate, effortful way of someone who understands, without quite admitting it, that stillness is dangerous. But the nights were difficult almost immediately. He would surface from sleep in a cold sweat, the smell of burning still somehow present in the room, his heart already hammering before he was fully conscious. He rarely remembered the dreams in detail, only the feeling they left behind — a certainty, residual and animal, that he was about to die.

Driving helps, up to a point. The cab is enclosed, the mirrors give him sight lines in every direction, and he can see who gets on. He has developed small rituals around this: he watches each passenger's hands before he watches their face. He is not sure when this started. He knows it is not entirely rational. He does it anyway.

There are days when the route feels manageable, even quietly satisfying. Then there are days when a lorry backfires in traffic and Marcus has to grip the steering wheel hard enough to whiten his knuckles, breathing through his nose until the shaking in his hands subsides. He has pulled over twice, telling passengers there was a mechanical fault, because he could not trust himself to continue. He has never told his supervisor.

He does not talk about Callum. He has not spoken his name aloud since the memorial service. When Callum's face appears to him — and it does, without invitation, at the bus depot, in the supermarket, in the mirror sometimes — Marcus feels something he cannot name precisely, somewhere between grief and guilt and a hot, formless shame. He has turned over the question of whether he should have seen something on that road, whether he missed a sign, more times than he can count. He has never arrived at an answer that satisfies him.

He has one close friend from before the army, a man named Joel, who invites him to things Marcus usually declines. He tells Joel he is tired from shifts. This is partly true. What is also true is that crowded pubs make him feel cornered, that loud music raises something in his chest that takes hours to settle, and that he finds it increasingly hard to sit with people who have no idea what he is carrying.

Marcus is twenty-one. He drives the same six miles, day after day, and he watches the hands of the people who get on.
